candidates.statement: This guidance provides recommendations for replacing color additives 2 in approved or marketed 19 drug products. If a color additive is used in a drug product, the color additive must conform to 20 FDA’s color additive regulations. 3 If FDA deems the color additive unsafe 4 and repeals 5 the 21 color additive regulation, the color additive must be removed or replaced. Color additives can 22 also be replaced for other reasons (e.g., as a business decision). 23

candidates.statement: The FD&C Act defines a color additive as any dye, pigment, or other substance that can impart 86 color to a food, drug, cosmetic, or the human body. 17 Color additives used in a drug are deemed 87 unsafe and prohibited except to the extent that FDA approves their use. 18 Color additives used in 88 approved or marketed drugs must be listed in the color additive regulations. 19 If FDA changes 89 the color additive regulations (e.g., removing a color additive), drug products that no longer 90 comply with the regulations must be updated to conform with the regulations. 20 If FDA removes 91 a color additive from the regulations, any drug product containing that additive will be 92 considered adulterated and cannot be marketed. 21 The introduction or delivery for introduction of 93 an adulterated drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act. 22 Furthermore, FDA may refuse 94 entry of a drug if it is or appears to be adulterated, unapproved, or otherwise fails to meet 95 applicable requirements. 23
candidates.context: A drug product is also considered adulterated if the drug product contains a color additive that is 98 not listed for such use (e.g., use of a color additive in an oral formulation when the color additive 99 is only authorized for use in topical drugs) or if the drug product fails to comply with the 100 statutory and regulatory requirements. 24 The manufacturing of drug products, including changes 101

candidates.statement: to production and process control procedures to replace a color additive, must comply with 102 CGMP requirements. 25 The firm’s change control procedures should include, but are not limited 103 to, the activities described in Sections V and VI to evaluate the effects of the color additive 104 change and the associated implementation activities. 105
candidates.context: 24 See section 501(a)(2)(B) and (a)(4) of the FD&C Act.

candidates.statement: Although changes to the “qualitative or quantitative formulation of the drug product, including 110 inactive ingredients,” are generally considered major changes, 26 in many cases, replacing a color 111 additive with one that is listed in the color additive regulations is unlikely to have an adverse 112 effect on the identity, strength, quality, purity, or potency of the drug product. Therefore, for a 113 drug product marketed under an NDA or ANDA, replacing a color additive can generally be 114 considered a moderate change that applicants can submit in a CBE-30. 27 , 28 However, if changes 115 are made other than replacing a color additive and making the associated adjustments in 116 excipient levels described in this section, a CBE-30 may not be appropriate and a prior approval 117 supplement may be warranted. 29 A CBE-30 must be submitted at least 30 days before 118 distribution of the postchange drug product. 30 To submit a CBE-30 for a color additive 119 replacement, the change should not include: 120
candidates.context: • Changes in the levels of other inactive ingredients that exceed 5 percent of the target unit 122 dose weight. 31

candidates.statement: When selecting a replacement color additive, manufacturers and applicants should review the 144 color additive regulations. They must ensure that the color additive regulations list the proposed 145 color for use in drugs and that the proposed level and use conform to the regulations. 38 Certain 146 color additive regulations restrict the allowable levels of color additives. For example, 21 CFR 147 73.1200(c) restricts the total amount of elemental iron per day. Manufacturers and applicants that 148 remove or replace a color additive should also ensure that drug product strengths remain 149 distinguishable to help prevent medication errors (e.g., when drug products such as tablets are 150 marketed in multiple strengths). 151
candidates.context: V. SELECTING A REPLACEMENT COLOR ADDITIVE 142 Manufacturers and applicants can check the Inactive Ingredient Database (IID) 39 for additional 153 information, including the levels of color additives that have been used in FDA-approved drug 154 products. Although this information can be useful, color additives and levels of color additives 155 that are not listed in the IID can be acceptable if the color additive is listed in the regulations and 156 is used within the regulation’s restrictions. 157

candidates.statement: The in vitro data recommendations above assume that no other changes are made that would 201 necessitate in vivo bioequivalence studies. 49 If the previous color additive provided additional 202 functions, the assessment of the change should include pharmaceutical development studies. 203 These studies should be done to ensure that the replacement color additive provides the same 204 functions and that the drug product meets applicable quality standards. For example, if the color 205 additive’s opacity protects the active pharmaceutical ingredient or drug product from light 206 degradation, appropriate test methods to assess the stability of the formulation would include 207 tests to ensure that the replacement color additive provides similar protection. 50 Manufacturers of 208 over-the-counter monograph drug products must ensure that the replacement of the color additive 209 does not interfere with analytical methods routinely used to ensure consistent drug product 210 quality, such as release or stability tests. 51 Similarly, other manufacturers and applicants should 211 also ensure that the color additive does not interfere with the analytical methods. 212
